questions.q: What is the most common childhood cancer, accounting for approximately 30% of all pediatric malignancies?
questions.hint: Leukemia accounts for roughly 30% of all childhood cancers.
questions.explanation: Leukemia is the most frequent cancer in children, representing approximately 30% of all pediatric malignancies.

questions.q: Which disease subtype accounts for the vast majority (75–80%) of pediatric leukemia cases?
questions.hint: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) makes up 75–80% of childhood leukemias.
questions.explanation: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) comprises 75–80% of all childhood leukemias, making it the single most common pediatric cancer.

questions.q: What is the peak age of incidence for Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor)?
options: B) 2 to 5 years (with a peak at 3 years)
questions.hint: Most commonly seen between 2 and 5 years, peaking around age 3.
questions.explanation: Nephroblastoma is most commonly diagnosed between 2 and 5 years of age, with a peak incidence occurring at 3 years of age.

questions.q: From which embryonic cell line does Neuroblastoma originate?
options: D) Neural crest cells arising in the adrenal medulla or sympathetic ganglia
questions.hint: Neural crest cells forming the adrenal medulla and sympathetic ganglia.
questions.explanation: Neuroblastoma is an embryonal tumor originating from neural crest cells that migrate to form the adrenal medulla (50% of cases) and sympathetic ganglia.

questions.q: What is the hallmark microscopic diagnostic cell identified in Hodgkin Lymphoma?
options: D) Small round blue uniform lymphoblasts
questions.hint: Reed-Sternberg cells are the hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma.
questions.explanation: The diagnostic hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma is the Reed-Sternberg cell, which is a large cancerous cell containing more than one nucleus.

questions.q: Which microscopic pattern is classic for Burkitt Lymphoma cytology on tissue biopsy or aspirate?
questions.hint: Tingible-body macrophages amid lymphoid cells give a 'starry sky' pattern.
questions.explanation: Cytological aspirate or biopsy of Burkitt lymphoma displays abnormal vacuolated lymphoid cells interspersed with tangible-body macrophages, yielding a classic 'starry sky' appearance.

questions.q: Where does Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor) primarily originate?
options: A) Renal parenchyma originating from nephrogenic blastema
questions.hint: Renal parenchyma from persistent nephrogenic blastema.
questions.explanation: Wilms tumor is a malignant embryonal tumor of the kidney originating from persistent nephrogenic blastema.

questions.q: What percentage of childhood malignancies is accounted for by lymphomas overall?
questions.hint: Roughly 14% of childhood malignancies are lymphomas.
questions.explanation: Lymphomas account for about 14% of all childhood malignancies, divided roughly equally between Hodgkin and Non-Hodgkin lymphomas.

questions.q: Which tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 11p13 is implicated in Wilms tumor tumorigenesis?
questions.hint: WT1 on chromosome 11p13.
questions.explanation: The WT1 gene, located on chromosome 11p13, is directly implicated in the embryological development of the genitourinary tract and Wilms tumor tumorigenesis.

questions.q: In developing countries, when does the early age peak of Hodgkin lymphoma typically manifest?
questions.hint: In developing settings, the early peak occurs before adolescence.
questions.explanation: In developing nations, the initial age peak of Hodgkin lymphoma occurs early in childhood before adolescence, unlike in high-resource settings where it peaks in young adulthood.

questions.q: How do Wilms tumor and Neuroblastoma typically differ regarding whether the abdominal mass crosses the anatomic midline?
options: A) Wilms tumor crosses the midline; Neuroblastoma stays strictly unilateral
B) Wilms tumor is smooth, firm, and does NOT cross the midline; Neuroblastoma is hard, irregular, and frequently crosses the midline
C) Both tumors cross the midline in 100% of cases
D) Neither tumor forms a palpable abdominal mass
questions.hint: Wilms is smooth/firm and stays unilateral; neuroblastoma is hard/irregular and crosses the midline.
questions.explanation: Wilms tumor typically presents as a smooth, firm, non-tender intra-renal mass that does not cross the abdominal aortic midline. In contrast, Neuroblastoma presents as a hard, nodular, fixed mass that frequently crosses the midline.

questions.q: Which genetic subtype of B-ALL represents the single most common favorable genetic abnormality, present in 25–30% of pediatric cases?
questions.hint: High hyperdiploidy (>50 chromosomes) is common in B-ALL and carries a favorable prognosis.
questions.explanation: High hyperdiploidy (>50 chromosomes, often with trisomies 4, 10, and 17) carries a favorable prognosis and represents 25–30% of pediatric B-ALL cases.

questions.q: What specific syndrome features Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genital/urinary malformations, and Intellectual disability?
questions.hint: Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies, and intellectual disability = WAGR.
questions.explanation: WAGR syndrome is a congenital deletion syndrome defined by Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies, and Range of intellectual disability (mental Retardation).

questions.q: Which classic clinical sign describes the periorbital ecchymosis and proptosis resulting from orbital bone metastases in Neuroblastoma?
questions.hint: Orbital metastases in neuroblastoma cause 'raccoon eyes'.
questions.explanation: Retrobulbar and orbital bone metastases in Neuroblastoma produce proptosis and periorbital ecchymosis, clinically described as 'raccoon eyes'.

questions.q: What urinary catecholamine metabolites are elevated in >90% of children with Neuroblastoma?
options: B) Homovanillic acid (HVA) and Vanillylmandelic acid (VMA)
questions.hint: Urinary HVA and VMA.
questions.explanation: Neuroblastoma tumor cells synthesize and metabolize catecholamines, leading to elevated urinary excretion of Homovanillic Acid (HVA) and Vanillylmandelic Acid (VMA) in over 90% of patients.

questions.q: Which classic fever pattern is characterized by high temperature for several days alternating with afebrile periods in Hodgkin Lymphoma?
questions.hint: Pel-Ebstein fever cycles between high fever and afebrile intervals.
questions.explanation: Pel-Ebstein fever is a systemic manifestation of Hodgkin lymphoma characterized by recurring cycles of high fever for several days alternating with days or weeks of normal or subnormal temperatures.

questions.q: What is the most common presenting anatomical site for Endemic Burkitt Lymphoma in African children?
options: D) Maxilla or mandible (jaw tumor causing facial swelling)
questions.hint: Jaw mass involving the maxilla or mandible.
questions.explanation: Endemic Burkitt lymphoma in equatorial Africa presents most frequently as a rapidly growing jaw tumor involving the maxilla or mandible, causing facial gross swelling and tooth displacement.

questions.q: What proportion of childhood leukemia cases is represented by Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)?
questions.hint: AML accounts for roughly 15–20% of childhood leukemias.
questions.explanation: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) represents approximately 15–20% of pediatric leukemia cases.

questions.q: Which targeted regimen is indicated for treating Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL, PML::RARA)?
options: B) All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) plus Arsenic Trioxide (ATO)
C) Vincristine and Actinomycin D only
questions.hint: ATRA plus arsenic trioxide (ATO) for APL.
questions.explanation: APL (with PML::RARA fusion) is treated with target-directed differentiation therapy using All-Trans Retinoic Acid (ATRA) plus Arsenic Trioxide (ATO), yielding cure rates >90–95%.

questions.q: Which Rye classification subtype accounts for the largest proportion (46%) of pediatric Hodgkin Lymphoma cases?
questions.hint: Nodular sclerosing (NS) is the most common Rye subtype (~46%).
questions.explanation: Under the Rye classification for Hodgkin lymphoma, Nodular Sclerosing (NS) is the most frequent subtype, making up 46% of cases.

questions.q: What paraneoplastic syndrome associated with Neuroblastoma presents with myoclonic jerking, random multi-vectorial eye movements, and ataxia?
questions.hint: Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome (OMAS).
questions.explanation: Opsoclonus-Myoclonus-Ataxia Syndrome (OMAS) is an autoimmune paraneoplastic neurological condition triggered by neuroblastoma, featuring rapid chaotic eye movements, muscular myoclonus, and cerebellar ataxia.

questions.q: Under the SIOP treatment protocol used in Tanzania for Wilms tumor, what is the initial management sequence?
options: A) Pre-operative Chemotherapy (Vincristine + Actinomycin D) FIRST to shrink the tumor, followed by Nephrectomy
B) Immediate radical nephrectomy followed by observation alone
C) External beam radiation therapy as the sole initial treatment
D) High-dose oral corticosteroids for 6 months
questions.hint: SIOP starts with pre-operative chemotherapy (vincristine + actinomycin D) before nephrectomy.
questions.explanation: The SIOP protocol utilizes 4–6 weeks of pre-operative chemotherapy (Vincristine + Actinomycin D) first to shrink the renal mass and reduce the risk of intraoperative tumor rupture before surgical nephrectomy.

questions.q: Which translocation fusion gene is a favorable prognostic marker in pediatric B-ALL, present in ~20–25% of cases?
questions.hint: ETV6::RUNX1 [t(12;21)] is a favorable B-ALL fusion gene.
questions.explanation: The ETV6::RUNX1 fusion gene [t(12;21)] occurs in 20–25% of B-ALL cases and confers a highly favorable prognosis.

questions.q: According to the St. Jude Staging System for Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma, what defines Stage IV?
options: A) Single tumor outside abdomen and mediastinum
B) Tumors on both sides of the diaphragm
C) Initial involvement of Bone Marrow or Central Nervous System (CNS) regardless of other sites
questions.hint: Bone marrow or CNS involvement at diagnosis defines St. Jude Stage IV.
questions.explanation: St. Jude Stage IV pediatric NHL is defined by the presence of bone marrow or CNS involvement, regardless of the extent of extra-nodal or nodal involvement elsewhere.

questions.q: What is the primary treatment modality for pediatric Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL)?
options: B) Radiation therapy to all nodal beds
D) Multiagent systemic chemotherapy combined with intrathecal chemotherapy
questions.hint: Multiagent systemic chemotherapy plus intrathecal chemotherapy.
questions.explanation: The primary treatment for childhood NHL is multiagent systemic chemotherapy combined with intrathecal chemotherapy to prevent or treat CNS disease.

questions.q: What nuclear medicine radionucleotide scan selectively targets neuroblastoma tissue via uptake into sympathetic adrenergic cells?
questions.hint: Iodine-123 MIBG scan.
questions.explanation: MIBG is a norepinephrine analog selectively taken up by sympathetic adrenergic tissues, making Iodine-123 MIBG scintigraphy highly specific for staging and monitoring neuroblastoma.

questions.q: In infants under 1 year of age, what special Neuroblastoma stage is characterized by a localized primary tumor with dissemination strictly limited to liver, skin, and/or bone marrow (<10% marrow tumor)?
questions.hint: Stage 4S / MS in infants <1 year with spread limited to skin, liver, and <10% marrow.
questions.explanation: Stage 4S (or MS) is restricted to infants <1 year of age who have a localized primary tumor with metastases confined to skin, liver, and/or minimal bone marrow (<10% involvement).

questions.q: What is the primary cause of bone marrow failure symptoms (anemia, bleeding, neutropenic fever) in pediatric acute leukemia?
options: A) Replacement of normal hematopoietic precursors by proliferating leukemic blast cells in the marrow
B) Autoimmune destruction of mature erythrocytes in the spleen
C) Renal erythropoietin deficiency from tumor compression
questions.hint: Leukemic blasts crowd out and replace normal bone marrow precursors.
questions.explanation: The progressive accumulation and overcrowding of leukemic blasts within the bone marrow cavity physically suppresses normal hematopoiesis, causing anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia.

questions.q: What percentage of blast cells in the bone marrow or blood is required to establish a diagnosis of Acute Leukemia according to WHO criteria?
questions.hint: ≥20% blasts by WHO criteria.
questions.explanation: WHO criteria define acute leukemia by the demonstration of 20% or more immature blasts in the bone marrow or peripheral blood.

questions.q: Which combination chemotherapy regimen includes doxorubicin, vinblastine, mechlorethamine, vincristine, bleomycin, etoposide, and prednisone for advanced pediatric Hodgkin lymphoma?
questions.hint: Stanford V.
questions.explanation: The Stanford V protocol incorporates doxorubicin, vinblastine, mechlorethamine, vincristine, bleomycin, etoposide, and prednisone for advanced pediatric Hodgkin lymphoma.

questions.q: What life-threatening medical emergency can occur during initial chemotherapy induction for high-burden malignancies (Burkitt lymphoma, ALL) due to rapid cell breakdown?
options: A) Tumor Lysis Syndrome (hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, hypocalcemia)
questions.hint: Tumor lysis syndrome: high K+, high PO4, high uric acid, low Ca2+.
questions.explanation: Tumor Lysis Syndrome results from rapid massive lysis of malignant cells, releasing intracellular potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids (converted to uric acid) into the circulation, precipitating acute renal failure and lethal arrhythmias.

questions.q: What specific medication is administered during Burkitt lymphoma chemotherapy to prevent hyperuricemia and acute uric acid nephropathy in Tumor Lysis Syndrome?
questions.hint: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase to lower uric acid.
questions.explanation: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, blocking the conversion of purines to uric acid, and is co-administered during induction therapy for Burkitt lymphoma to prevent tumor lysis nephropathy.

questions.q: How does Favorable Histology Wilms tumor differ from Unfavorable (Anaplastic) Histology Wilms tumor under the microscope?
options: A) Favorable exhibits Homer-Wright pseudorosettes; Unfavorable exhibits Reed-Sternberg cells
B) Favorable exhibits minimal cellular pleomorphism and has a >90% cure rate; Unfavorable exhibits deformed, anaplastic cells and is much harder to cure
C) Favorable contains 100% necrosis; Unfavorable contains zero mitosis
D) Favorable is found only in adults; Unfavorable is found only in newborns
questions.hint: Unfavorable histology shows anaplastic/deformed cells and carries a worse prognosis than favorable histology.
questions.explanation: Favorable histology Wilms tumor lacks severe nuclear atypia or anaplasia and carries a cure rate >90%, whereas unfavorable (anaplastic) histology features bizarre pleomorphic nuclei and is resistant to standard therapy.

questions.q: Which pediatric leukemia subtype is strongly associated with Down syndrome (Trisomy 21)?
options: A) Both ALL and Acute Megakaryoblastic Leukemia / AML
questions.hint: Trisomy 21 increases risk for both ALL and AML (especially acute megakaryoblastic leukemia).
questions.explanation: Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) carries a significantly increased risk of developing acute leukemia, specifically Acute Megakaryoblastic Leukemia (AML M7) in early infancy and ALL in older children.

questions.q: Which targeted monoclonal antibody directs cytotoxic T-cells to CD19-positive B-ALL blasts (bispecific T-cell engager) and significantly improves survival in pediatric B-ALL?
questions.hint: Blinatumomab targets CD19.
questions.explanation: Blinatumomab is a bispecific T-cell engager (BiTE) antibody connecting T-cells to CD19 on B-ALL blasts, proven to improve disease-free survival in pediatric B-ALL.

questions.q: Which imaging modality is superior for visualizing intra-spinal extension ('dumbbell tumor') through neural foramina in Neuroblastoma?
questions.hint: MRI best evaluates soft tissue and spinal canal extension.
questions.explanation: MRI provides resolution of soft tissues and spinal canal anatomy, making it the modality of choice for identifying intra-spinal extension of paraspinal neuroblastomas ('dumbbell tumors').

questions.q: What is the role of surgery in pediatric Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL)?
options: A) Surgery is the primary curative modality for all stages
B) Surgery is used to debulk all intra-abdominal masses prior to chemotherapy
C) Surgery is used mainly for diagnostic/biologic tissue sampling and staging, and rarely for debulking large masses
D) Surgery is strictly contraindicated in all cases of NHL
questions.hint: Surgery in NHL is mainly for biopsy and staging rather than tumor debulking.
questions.explanation: Because pediatric NHL is highly chemotherapy-sensitive, surgery is limited to diagnostic tissue biopsies and staging, rarely serving a primary debulking role.

questions.q: What proportion of children with Neuroblastoma present with metastatic disease at the time of initial diagnosis?
questions.hint: More than 70% have metastatic spread at diagnosis.
questions.explanation: Neuroblastoma is clinically aggressive; over 70% of children have widespread metastatic disease (to bone, marrow, liver, or lymph nodes) at the time of initial presentation.

questions.q: Which clinical presentation of Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) manifests as a localized extramedullary mass of myeloid blast cells in soft tissues or orbit?
questions.hint: Myeloid sarcoma (chloroma).
questions.explanation: A myeloid sarcoma (historically termed chloroma) is an extramedullary tumor mass composed of immature myeloid blasts occurring in soft tissue, bone, orbit, or skin.

questions.q: What advantage does Proton Beam Radiation Therapy offer over conventional external beam radiation in pediatric Hodgkin lymphoma?
options: A) It eliminates the need for multi-agent chemotherapy
B) It can be administered orally at home
C) It uses positively charged proton streams that deposit energy precisely at the target, reducing radiation damage to surrounding healthy tissues (heart, lungs, breasts)
D) It guarantees 100% cure in refractory Stage IV disease without side effects
questions.hint: Precise energy deposition spares nearby organs like the heart, lungs, and breasts.
questions.explanation: Proton beam therapy utilizes charged protons that release most of their energy at a defined depth (Bragg peak), reducing radiation scatter to developing pediatric organs like the heart, lungs, and breast tissue.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with a painless, smooth, firm abdominal mass in the left flank that does NOT cross the midline, microscopic hematuria, hypertension, and an intra-renal mass on ultrasound. Identify the malignancy, the characteristic CT sign of distorted remnant renal tissue, and the initial SIOP treatment approach.
options: A) Neuroblastoma; 'Raccoon eyes' sign; Immediate radical nephrectomy followed by radiotherapy
B) Lymphoma; 'Starry sky' sign; High-dose intrathecal methotrexate alone
C) Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor); 'Claw' sign on CT; Pre-operative chemotherapy (Vincristine + Actinomycin D) for 4–6 weeks to shrink the tumor, followed by Nephrectomy and lymph node sampling
D) Hepatoblastoma; 'Double bubble' sign; Liver transplantation
questions.hint: Intra-renal mass not crossing midline + 'claw sign' = Wilms tumor; SIOP uses pre-op vincristine + actinomycin D before nephrectomy.
questions.explanation: A smooth intra-renal mass in a 3-year-old that does not cross the midline with hematuria/hypertension is classic for Wilms tumor. CT shows the 'claw sign' of distorted normal kidney tissue stretched around the tumor. Under SIOP, treatment starts with pre-operative Vincristine + Actinomycin D followed by nephrectomy.

questions.q: A 14-month-old infant presents with fever, weight loss, an irregular hard abdominal mass crossing the midline, proptosis with periorbital ecchymosis ('raccoon eyes'), opsoclonus-myoclonus, and elevated urinary VMA and HVA. Identify the diagnosis, tissue of origin, and how its mass differs physically from Wilms tumor.
options: A) Nephroblastoma; Metanephric blastema; Smooth, ballotable mass that stays on one side
B) Neuroblastoma; Neural crest cells (sympathetic chain / adrenal medulla); Hard, irregular, nodular mass that CROSSES the midline
C) Burkitt Lymphoma; Mature T-lymphocytes; Soft cystic mass in the anterior mediastinum
D) Acute Myeloid Leukemia; Myeloid stem cells; Generalized soft lymphadenopathy
questions.hint: Raccoon eyes + opsoclonus-myoclonus + high VMA/HVA = neuroblastoma from neural crest cells; hard, irregular, crosses midline.
questions.explanation: An infant with raccoon eyes, opsoclonus-myoclonus, elevated VMA/HVA, and a hard abdominal mass crossing the midline has Neuroblastoma, arising from neural crest cells. Unlike Wilms tumor, Neuroblastoma is hard, irregular, and crosses the midline.

questions.q: A 4-year-old girl presents with pallor, low-grade fever, purpura, bone pain/limp, Hb 6.2 g/dL, platelets 18,000/µL, and WBC 45,000/µL with 65% lymphoblasts. What is the likely diagnosis, the mandatory diagnostic procedure, and the four treatment phases?
options: A) Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL); Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy (≥20–25% blasts); Induction, Consolidation/Intensification, Interim Maintenance, and Prolonged Maintenance therapy
B) Hodgkin Lymphoma; Excisional lymph node biopsy; Surgery, Radiation, Chemotherapy, Immunotherapy
C) Neuroblastoma; MIBG scan; Low-risk, Intermediate-risk, High-risk, and Relapse phases
D) Aplastic Anemia; Peripheral blood film; Immunosuppression, Steroids, Transfusion, and Discharge
questions.hint: Cytopenias + lymphoblasts = ALL; confirmed by bone marrow aspirate/biopsy; treated in 4 phases.
questions.explanation: Bone marrow failure + bone pain + circulating lymphoblasts indicates ALL. Diagnosis requires bone marrow aspirate/biopsy demonstrating ≥20–25% blasts. Treatment follows 4 phases: Induction, Consolidation, Interim Maintenance, and Maintenance.

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy in East Africa presents with a rapidly enlarging left jaw mass causing facial swelling and tooth loosening, with vacuolated lymphoid cells on cytology. Identify the lymphoma subtype, viral association, cytological pattern, and acute metabolic complication to prevent during treatment.
options: A) Hodgkin Lymphoma (Nodular Sclerosing); Cytomegalovirus; Reed-Sternberg reaction; Hypocalcemic tetany
B) T-cell Lymphoblastic Lymphoma; Human T-lymphotropic virus; Homer-Wright pseudorosette; Hypokalemia
C) Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma; Hepatitis B virus; Onion-skin pattern; Hepatic encephalopathy
D) Endemic Burkitt Lymphoma; Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) association; 'Starry sky' microscopic pattern; Tumor Lysis Syndrome (treated with Allopurinol and hydration)
questions.hint: Jaw mass in East Africa = endemic Burkitt lymphoma (EBV, 'starry sky' pattern); prevent tumor lysis syndrome with allopurinol and hydration.
questions.explanation: An endemic jaw tumor in East Africa is classic for Burkitt Lymphoma, associated with EBV and displaying a 'starry sky' pattern. Rapid chemo-induced cell lysis causes Tumor Lysis Syndrome, requiring Allopurinol and vigorous hydration.

questions.q: A 15-year-old boy presents with painless firm cervical/supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, night sweats, Pel-Ebstein fever, 12% weight loss, a mediastinal mass, and binucleated cells with prominent nucleoli on biopsy. Diagnose the malignancy, classify the systemic symptoms, and name the hallmark cell.
options: A) Hodgkin Lymphoma; Positive B symptoms (Fever, Night sweats, Weight loss >10%); Reed-Sternberg cells
B) Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma; Absence of B symptoms; Lymphoblasts
C) Neuroblastoma; Category C symptoms; Small round blue cells
D) Infectious Mononucleosis; Non-specific viral symptoms; Atypical T-lymphocytes
questions.hint: Pel-Ebstein fever, night sweats, >10% weight loss, and Reed-Sternberg cells = Hodgkin lymphoma with B symptoms.
questions.explanation: Firm rubbery cervical nodes with Pel-Ebstein fever, night sweats, and >10% weight loss define Hodgkin Lymphoma with B symptoms. Biopsy confirms diagnostic Reed-Sternberg cells.

questions.q: A 16-year-old male with T-cell ALL presents with severe dyspnea, orthopnea, facial edema, neck/chest venous distension, and a large anterior mediastinal mass. Identify the acute oncological emergency, the risk with sedation/anesthesia, and urgent management.
options: A) Cardiac Tamponade; Myocardial rupture; Perform immediate pericardiocentesis
B) Tension Pneumothorax; Lung collapse; Insert intercostal chest drain
C) Pulmonary Embolism; Right heart failure; Administer IV tissue plasminogen activator

D) Superior Vena Cava (SVC) Syndrome / Complete Airway Compression; Fatal airway collapse or severe cardiovascular instability upon muscular relaxation; Administer prompt oxygen, avoid supine positioning/sedation, and initiate urgent corticosteroids or targeted chemotherapy
questions.hint: Anterior mediastinal mass + dyspnea/venous congestion = SVC syndrome/airway compression; avoid supine/sedation, give O2 and urgent steroids/chemo.
questions.explanation: Mediastinal mass in T-ALL causing upper body congestion and respiratory distress is SVC Syndrome / Airway Compression. Sedation causes loss of chest wall tone leading to fatal airway collapse; management requires upright posture, oxygen, and rapid steroid/chemo administration.

questions.q: A 2-year-old with high-risk B-ALL achieves morphologic complete remission (<5% blasts) after Induction, but end-of-induction flow cytometry shows 0.8% minimal residual disease (MRD). What is the clinical significance of persistent MRD, how does it affect therapy, and what targeted immunotherapy is indicated?
options: A) MRD is irrelevant if morphologic remission is achieved; Continue standard maintenance without changes; No immunotherapy needed
B) MRD is a weak factor; Reduce chemotherapy doses to prevent toxicity; Administer oral steroids
C) MRD indicates terminal disease; Stop all chemotherapy and initiate palliative care
D) MRD is the single strongest prognostic factor for relapse risk; Mandates treatment intensification (re-stratification to higher risk arm) and consideration of Blinatumomab or CAR T-cell therapy
questions.hint: Persistent MRD predicts relapse; intensify therapy and consider blinatumomab or CAR T-cell therapy.
questions.explanation: End-of-induction MRD is the strongest predictor of relapse. Persistent MRD (≥0.01%) requires treatment intensification and targeted immunotherapies like Blinatumomab or CD19 CAR T-cell therapy.

questions.q: In comparing Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor) and Neuroblastoma on cross-sectional CT imaging: which tumor shows fine stippled calcifications in >80% of cases, which encases/displaces abdominal vessels, and which produces the 'claw sign' of compressed renal parenchyma?
options: A) 1. Wilms tumor; 2. Wilms tumor; 3. Neuroblastoma
B) 1. Neuroblastoma (calcifications common); 2. Neuroblastoma (encases vessels, crosses midline); 3. Wilms tumor ('claw sign' of renal parenchyma)
questions.hint: Neuroblastoma = calcifications and encasing vessels; Wilms = 'claw sign' of renal tissue.
questions.explanation: CT imaging differentiates the two tumors: Neuroblastoma shows stippled calcifications and encases/displaces abdominal vessels while crossing the midline. Wilms tumor originates within the kidney, expanding to produce the 'claw sign' of compressed renal parenchyma.

questions.q: A 9-month-old infant presents with massive hepatomegaly, bluish skin nodules ('blueberry muffin' sign), <10% marrow blasts, and a 2 cm left adrenal mass without vascular encasement. What stage of Neuroblastoma is this, what is its typical behavior/prognosis, and how is it managed?
options: A) Stage IV; High risk; Require radical surgery, total body irradiation, and stem cell transplant
B) Stage I; Low risk; Requires immediate total hepatectomy
C) Stage III; Intermediate risk; Requires 2 years of intensive multi-agent chemotherapy

D) Stage 4S (INSS) / Stage MS (INRG); High rate of spontaneous regression with excellent overall survival (>80–90%); Managed conservatively with observation or minimal low-dose chemotherapy if organ function is compromised
questions.hint: Infant <1 year with localized tumor + liver/skin/<10% marrow spread = Stage 4S/MS; high spontaneous regression, mainly observation.
questions.explanation: An infant <1 year with localized primary neuroblastoma and metastases limited to liver, skin, and <10% marrow has Stage 4S / MS. This stage exhibits a high rate of spontaneous regression and excellent survival, treated primarily with observation.

questions.q: For a 5-year-old child with acute leukemia: what bone marrow diagnostic panel is mandatory, how do flow cytometry markers distinguish B-ALL, T-ALL, and AML, and what is the 5-year overall survival benchmark for pediatric ALL in high-resource settings?
options: A) 1. Bone marrow aspirate/biopsy for Morphology, Flow Cytometry, Cytogenetics (FISH), and Molecular Genetics; 2. B-ALL (CD19, CD10, CD22), T-ALL (cytoplasmic/surface CD3, CD7), AML (MPO, CD13, CD33, CD117); 3. >90% 5-year overall survival
B) 1. Stool culture and urine dipstick; 2. All leukemias express identical surface receptors; 3. Less than 10%
C) 1. Lumbar puncture alone; 2. Distinguished by peripheral blood count only; 3. Exactly 50%
D) 1. Lymph node biopsy alone; 2. Distinguished by chest X-ray findings; 3. 100% without treatment
questions.hint: Morphology, flow cytometry, cytogenetics, molecular genetics; B-ALL (CD19/10/22), T-ALL (CD3/7), AML (MPO/CD13/33/117); >90% survival.
questions.explanation: Diagnosis requires bone marrow aspirate/biopsy for morphology, flow cytometry, cytogenetics, and molecular genetics. Flow cytometry assigns lineage: B-ALL (CD19, CD10, CD22), T-ALL (CD3, CD7), and AML (MPO, CD13, CD33, CD117). 5-year overall survival for pediatric ALL now exceeds 90% in high-resource settings.
